notes.meaning: Good King Jehoshaphat died and was buried with his family in Jerusalem, the City of David. His son Jehoram took the throne. Matthew Henry says Judah never changed kings so badly: one of the best kings was followed by one of the worst. Jehoshaphat had arranged for Jehoram to marry Ahab's daughter, and the harm from that marriage showed only after he died.

Jehoram had six brothers. Two were named Azariah, but the names are spelled a little differently in Hebrew, so people could tell them apart. Jehoshaphat is called "king of Israel" even though he ruled Judah. Older writers explain this in different ways. Many Israelites from the north had moved into his land, and he ruled God's people as a true king of Israel should. Some think a copyist simply wrote "Israel" for "Judah."

Jehoshaphat gave his younger sons rich gifts and put each in charge of a strong, walled city. This gave them an honorable living. It also kept them spread out and content, so they would not trouble the heir. The crown went to Jehoram because he was the oldest. Matthew Henry wonders whether it was wise to hand the kingdom to a son who was so unfit to rule.

Once Jehoram felt secure, he murdered all his brothers and some leading officials. Matthew Henry compares him to Cain: their goodness shamed his wickedness. Keil & Delitzsch think the brothers likely opposed his turn to idol worship, since verse 13 calls them better than he was. The officials may have been faithful men who would have spoken against him. The Jewish historian Josephus says his wife Athaliah urged him on.

Jehoram was 32 when he became king, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem. Adam Clarke explains that he shared the throne with his father for a few years first. So he ruled alone only about five years. It was a short and unhappy reign.

Jehoram copied the wicked kings of the northern kingdom, Israel. The reason is given: he married Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel. Clarke thinks she was probably the main cause of his cruelty and his turning from God. Her influence soon wiped out all his good father had taught him. The Geneva Notes draw the lesson that we cannot join ourselves to the wicked and still serve God.

Jehoram deserved to have his family wiped out, but God held back. God had made a covenant with David. A covenant is a binding promise. God had promised to keep a "lamp" burning for David, which means always giving him a descendant on the throne. David's family could be punished for sin, but the promise would not be broken. Matthew Henry notes that a great blessing was in that family line: the coming Messiah.
Edom, the nation south of Judah, had been under Judah's control since David's time and paid it tribute. Now it saw that Judah was weak under Jehoram, so it broke free and chose its own king.

Jehoram marched into Edom with his officers and chariots. When the Edomites surrounded him, he broke out with an attack by night. He won that fight, but he could not bring Edom back under his rule. Guzik thinks the battle may not have settled anything.

Edom stayed free from then on. Libnah, a town near Judah's border, also broke away. The writer gives the real reason: Jehoram had abandoned the LORD. Matthew Henry and Wesley put it this way: while he held to God, his people held to him; when he cast God off, they cast him off. Whatever the rebels' motives, God allowed it as a judgment on Jehoram.

Jehoram built "high places," which were hilltop shrines for false gods. His father and grandfather had torn these down. The Bible calls idol worship "prostitution" because God's people belonged to Him like a wife to her husband. Turning to other gods was unfaithfulness to Him. Jehoram did more than set a bad example. He used his power to force the people into it.

A written message came from the prophet Elijah. Many older writers think Elijah wrote it near the end of his life on earth and left it, perhaps with Elisha, to be delivered at the right time. Others think God showed him Jehoram's sins ahead of time. Some think the name should read Elisha. The letter speaks for "the God of your father David." It reminds Jehoram whose family he came from. It charges him with leaving his godly father's ways, following Ahab's family, leading Judah into idol worship, and murdering brothers who were better men than he was.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think the letter, in the form we have it, was written by a later historian. They believe he summed up in his own words how Elijah's message related to Jehoram's troubles.

notes.meaning: God announced two punishments. A heavy blow would fall on Jehoram's people, sons, wives and goods, because they had shared in his idol worship. Jehoram himself would suffer a long, painful bowel disease. Keil & Delitzsch link the first to his idolatry and the second to his murders. Matthew Henry notes that he was warned beforehand, so no one could call it chance. If he had humbled himself, as even Ahab once did, he might have found mercy.

God stirred up the Philistines and some Arab peoples to attack Judah. The Philistines had long been beaten down, but God gave them courage to carry out His judgment. Adam Clarke notes that we have no other record of this war.

The raiders took the king's goods, his wives and his sons. Only his youngest son, Jehoahaz (also called Ahaziah), was left. Matthew Henry and Wesley call it "blood for blood": he killed his brothers to make himself strong, and now he lost his sons. One son survived only because God had promised to keep David's line going.

After all this, the LORD struck Jehoram with a bowel disease no one could cure, just as the letter had warned. Matthew Henry notes that the man who showed no tender feeling for his brothers was struck in his inner parts. Henry adds that godly people may get sick too, but for them illness is a loving Father's correction, and God comforts them through it.

The illness dragged on for two years until his intestines came out, and he died in terrible pain. His people did not light the usual fire of sweet-smelling spices to honor him, as they had for earlier kings. This showed how little they thought of his evil reign.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read the hard Hebrew wording differently. They think it means the worst came suddenly at the very end, within about "two days," rather than after two years.

notes.meaning: Jehoram died, and no one was sorry. Wesley notes that people sometimes wish for a ruler's death and later regret it, but not this time. He was buried in Jerusalem but kept out of the royal tombs. That was a public judgment on how badly he had ruled. His name means "exalted by the LORD," yet his wickedness brought him to a shameful grave.
